primary.locator: Read 2B-2C on measurable spaces and measures, 3A-3B on integration and convergence, then 5B on iterated integrals. Consult 2D only when the construction of Lebesgue measure is the gap.

practice.label: Measurability, convergence and iterated-integral exercises
practice.availability: Exercises provided; public solutions not verified.
practice.locator: Exercises 2B, 2C, 3A, 3B and 5B, immediately following the named sections.

checks: On (0,1) with Lebesgue measure let f_n = n times the indicator of (0,1/n). Find the pointwise limit and each integral; prove that no single integrable function dominates all f_n.
Compute the integral of exp(-x-y) over 0 < x < y < infinity in both orders, stating which theorem permits the exchange.
measure-theory.skip: Skip this review if you can justify both checks and verify monotone or dominated convergence in a new example. Review measurable-space definitions separately if you know integration formulas but cannot prove a function measurable.

objectives: Use complex differentiability and Cauchy-Riemann equations with the required regularity hypotheses.
Apply Cauchy's formula to obtain derivatives and estimates.
Classify isolated singularities and compute residues.
Compare zero sets and holomorphic extension in one and several complex variables.

primary.title: Guide to Cultivating Complex Analysis: Working the Complex Field
primary.author: Jiří Lebl
primary.locator: Read 2.1 on holomorphic functions, 3.2-3.3 on Cauchy's theorem and consequences, 4.4 on Laurent series, and 5.1-5.4 on zeros, singularities and residues. Review line integrals in 3.1 if needed.

alternatives.title: Tasty Bits of Several Complex Variables: A Whirlwind Tour of the Subject
alternatives.author: Jiří Lebl
alternatives.locator: Sections 1.1-1.3 on functions, power series and derivatives; 1.6 on extension and zero sets; 2.1 on domains of holomorphy and holomorphic extension.
alternatives.purpose: Continue after one-variable Cauchy theory to see which familiar geometric conclusions change in several variables.

practice.label: Holomorphic-function and residue exercises
practice.availability: Exercises provided; public solutions not verified.
practice.locator: Exercises 2.1.1-2.1.6 for differentiability and Cauchy-Riemann; exercises embedded in sections 4.4 and 5.3 for Laurent series and residues.

checks: Determine every point where f(z) = absolute value of z squared is complex differentiable, using the derivative definition as well as the Cauchy-Riemann equations.
Compute the positively oriented unit-circle integral of exp(z)/z squared and identify the residue.
In C squared describe the zero set of f(z,w)=zw and show that its zeros are not isolated. Explain why this does not contradict the one-variable isolated-zero theorem.
complex-analysis.skip: Skip the one-variable selection if you can do the first two checks and state the domain hypotheses of Cauchy's theorem. Take the several-variable route only after that; skip it if extension phenomena and positive-dimensional zero sets are already familiar.

Compute norms of elementary bounded operators and functionals.

primary.title: Functional Analysis: Lecture Notes for 18.102
primary.author: Richard Melrose
primary.locator: Chapter 1, sections 2-6 and 8-12 for Banach spaces and the main operator theorems. Then chapter 3, sections 8-11 for projections and adjoints and 14-18 for compactness, weak convergence and the compact self-adjoint spectral theorem.

checks: On C[0,1] with the supremum norm compute the operator norm of L(f)=integral from 0 to 1 of t f(t) dt, proving both an upper bound and attainment.
On the complex Hilbert space ell squared, let Te_n=e_n/n for n>=1. Prove T is compact by finite-rank approximation and determine its spectrum, explaining the status of 0.
functional-analysis.skip: Skip Banach-space review if completeness and boundedness proofs are routine. Skip the Hilbert-space selection only if you can complete the compact-operator check and distinguish spectrum from point spectrum; finite-dimensional eigenvalue calculations alone do not suffice.

checkResults: A continuous image of a compact closed subset is compact and hence closed in the Hausdorff target; the inverse is continuous. The identity from discrete R to usual R is a counterexample without compactness.
The map t -> (cos(2pi t), sin(2pi t)) descends continuously by the quotient property and is bijective; compactness and Hausdorffness give a homeomorphism.

checkResults: The flow is (exp(-t)x0,exp(-2t)y0); V'=-2x squared-4y squared<=-2V. The rotation preserves V and has nonzero periodic orbits.

At 0 the multiplier is r: attractive for 0<r<1, repelling for r>1, inconclusive at r=1. For r>1 the second fixed point is 1-1/r with multiplier 2-r: attractive for 1<r<3, repelling for 3<r<=4, inconclusive at r=3. At r=1 the two formulas give the same fixed point.
